newsitem.title: USA: Anti-tobacco lawyer looking for second Florida win.
newsitem.headline: Anti-tobacco lawyer looking for second Florida win.

text.p: The stakes are higher this time around as the RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co. readies for a trial next week against the same lawyer who gave cigarette makers their worst courtroom loss in 40 years.
Investors, tobacco companies, lawyers and politicians will be watching Connor vs. RJ Reynolds to see if plaintiff attorney Norwood "Woody" Wilner can win two in a row.
Next week's trial, starting with jury selection Monday, is his first since last August, when he won a landmark $750,000 verdict in the same small Jacksonville courtroom.
The loser in last summer's trial, the Brown & Williamson unit of B.A.T Industries, has appealed the $750,000 award, which was made to a life-long smoker with lung cancer.

But the verdict hurt tobacco companies on Wall Street and emboldened anti-tobacco activists, who have filed hundreds of individual lawsuits. State governments also have sued the industry, seeking $30 billion in Medicaid costs. The industry is also under a regulatory assault by Washington.

Wilner said he will charge that Reynolds, America's second-largest cigarette maker, deceived the public with misleading ads. He is expected to use industry documents to argue Reynolds knowingly made a dangerous product and failed in its duty to warn users of its risks.

Reynolds' attorneys contend that the late Jean Connor, who died of cancer in 1995 at age 49, had made an informed decision to smoke. In a videotape recorded a few months before her death, she said she smoked because she "enjoyed it."
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for Connor's three children for mental anguish, medical, funeral and estate expenses and for lost wages.

Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Inc., also faces possible punitive damages. In Florida, punitive damage awards are usually capped at three times the amount of compensatory damages, But if judges find extraordinary circumstances, they can approve larger awards.

No tobacco company has faced such a courtroom risk, although the State of Florida has won a judge's go-ahead to seek punitive damages in its own suit claiming $1 billion or more spent on sick smokers through Medicaid.

Wilner said he expected to make no use in the trial of internal tobacco-industry documents which Liggett Group agreed to hand over to 22 state governments suing other tobacco companies. Wilner said he had seen of the Liggett papers but that they did not appear helpful to the Connor case.
Attorneys said choosing six jurors and three alternates could take several days. Circuit Judge Bernard Nachman has said the trial will last two to three weeks.

Wilner will try the case with Ron Motley of Charleston, S.C., and the two will rely heavily on the testimony of expert witness Dr. Allan Feingold, a pulmonary medicine specialist at South Miami Hospital.

Reynolds attorneys have sought to limit the areas in which Feingold can testify, and they will offer their own witnesses, including two University of California at Los Angeles medical school professors to testify that Connor's cancer cannot be conclusively linked to her smoking.
Reynolds lawyers are expected to argue that Connor was not an addict but someone who admitted that she liked to smoke and selected the brands she smoked based on their taste.
